Optimizing Garden Cress growth in Lunar Regolith Soil using an Automated Watering
System.

Background:
While pursuing sustainable living on the Moon, developing efficient agricultural practices
is imperative, especially for astronauts who are expecting to station long-term on the lunar
surface. Fortunately, NASA’s Artemis program aims to establish a semi-permanent lunar base,
which highlights the need for self-sufficient food production. Our primary focus became
nutritionally beneficial and small-scale crops like mini potatoes. However, as our experiment
progressed, we found that the mini-potatoes lacked any sign of growth. To combat this, we
shifted in focus and explored alternative options, such as the Garden Cress (Lepidium sativum),
which is known for its rapid growth and nutritional value: calorically low, packs vitamins A, C,
and K, and contains omega-3 fatty acids. Garden Cress also has been shown to aid immunity,
prevent diseases, facilitate organ function, decrease inflammation, and cater to heart health.
Furthermore, we used our team’s specific interest in engineering to integrate an automated
watering system, designed using the Arduino Uno Rev3 microcontroller board. The irrigation
system helped address the challenges in lunar farming, like irregular water supply and extreme
environmental conditions. Furthermore, this experiment was a great opportunity to pursue our
engineering passions, allowing us to blend botany and technology to engender sustainable
extraterrestrial agriculture.
Hypothesis:
As we increase the plant’s hydration and water, the Garden Cress will show increased signs of
growth.

Parameters:
Remaining constant for every part, our experimental design began with planting the
Garden Cress (Lepidium sativum), farming with a 1:1 ratio of moon stimulant and soli stimulant,
each approximately 230mL in volume. Our indoor UV light rested at approximately level 100,
and our pH level at 7pH was measured using the pH soil level meter provided. We’ve included
the circuit diagram for our automated watering system below, its components being the Arduino
board, wires, relay box, 9V battery, valve (motor), and a perforated pipe (connected to the pipe)
Variables:
Our Independent Variable is the quantity of water we administered to the plants. Our Dependent
Variable is the plant’s growth, the responsive measure to the changes in water quantity. Finally,
our Control Variables are the consistency in pot size, uniformity of plant species, soil
composition, and level of sunlight exposure.
Procedures:
1. Soak the Garden Cress seeds in a bowl of water for 24 hours (without sunlight)
1. Prepare a mixture of 50% moon simulant and 50% soil, then mix them equally into the
pots.
2. Place one spoon of seeds 1 inch below the surface of the soil in the pot
3. Place each pot under one hole of the pipe in order
4. Start the watering system (using the C++ code provided below)

void setup() {
pinMode(13, OUTPUT); // Set pin 13 as an output
}
void loop() {
digitalWrite(13, HIGH); // Valve opens
delay(10000); // Wait for 10 seconds
digitalWrite(13, LOW); // Valve closes
delay(86400000); // Wait for 24 hours (86400000 milliseconds)
}
Amount of water per pot (approx.):
Pot 1: No water
Pot 2: 1 tablespoon and 2 teaspoons
Pot 3: 4 tablespoons
Pot 4: 6 tablespoons
Pot 5: 8 tablespoons
Pot 6: One cup
Pot 7: 300 mL
Pot 8: 500 mL
Pot 9: 700 mL

Conclusion:
Our Hypothesis has been sustained. The plants receiving the highest water quantity
exhibited the most growth and leaf production. We discovered that this result was due to soil
moistness, and the Cress’s low fertilizer requirements in regards to the short growing time for

plants. This outcome supports our previous conjecture that plant growth would be directly
proportional to water quantity. Throughout the experiment, we have also uncovered that the
plant’s growth is quicker within the first couple of days of farming, as represented in the
logarithmic line of best fit.
Nevertheless, it is crucial to acknowledge the potential for errors. This is evident in the
initial interpretation of the plant growth graph, where the stems were reported as shorter than
previous days. This observation necessitates a thorough examination to identify and rectify any
errors that may have affected the accuracy of our discoveries.
This expirament was a valuable learning opportunity for our entire team, extending
beyond the realms of software engineering, mechatronics engineering, electrical engineering, and
data analysis. Beyond technical skills, the project provided a valuable lesson in fostering
collaboration and building rapport with our peers. Working collectively, we honed our ability to
collaboratively develop and implement efficient agricultural practices, highlighting the
importance of teamwork in the pursuit of innovative solutions.
